utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We shall continue our case. Can I have the number, Mr. Registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case number IT-95-14/1, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that I have learned of the sickness of Mr. Marchesiello. We wish him good health and a speedy recovery. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Marchesiello has been appointed to the bench in April. He will take up his appointment in April. He will no longer be returning to the Prosecutor's case. He has taken up a senior position. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, Ms. Sutherland and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic, representing, together with my colleague, Joka, the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we continue, Mr. Niemann, with the witness, of the Prosecution, I think. It is Mr. Meddegoda today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The first Prosecution witness this morning is the witness listed in paragraph 4; he is witness number 3 in paragraph 4 of the inventory of witnesses dated 20 March 1998 and, in respect of that witness, your Honours, I am seeking to apply for protective measures. The witness has indicated to me that he would wish to testify under a pseudonym and also the image of his face be distorted during the course of his testimony. Therefore, I move that your Honours be pleased to grant the protective measures sought by this witness. If your Honours are inclined to grant a pseudonym, the witness would be known as Witness L.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We were informed that the Defence has no objection to this. Is that true, Mr. Mikulicic, that you have no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Usher, can you bring down the blinds, please? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the solemn declaration that will be handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated, please. You are going to answer questions which the Prosecutor, Mr. Meddegoda, is going to put to you, if you please. WITNESS L Examined by MR. MEDDEGODA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Their Honours have been pleased to grant the protective measures you have sought before you testify before the Tribunal, and therefore you will be known as Witness L for the purposes of the record. Before you testify, I would hand over to you a sheet of paper, and I would ask you to look at the sheet of paper and confirm whether the name which appears on that sheet of paper is your name or not. May I please ask the usher to hand it over? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that could be shown to learned counsel for the Defence. Your Honours, I am moving to produce that sheet of paper with the witness's name as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be exhibit number 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness L, you are Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you state what your age is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in 1992, you served as a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, as a member of the TO, could you describe what your function was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My duties were mostly to keep watch in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were part of the village patrol, so to speak, as a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the TO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to be a member of the TO at the time the conflict broke out in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know between which parties the conflict broke out in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, between the HVO and the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on that day, on 27 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, members of the Croat Defence Council gave us an ultimatum that we should surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time was the ultimatum given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it when the ultimatum was given by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the day before -- I do not remember the exact date, but it could have been the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the ultimatum was given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not agree -- we sent a man to tell them -- tell the HVO that we would not surrender. He went, and they would not let him come back to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you and the other villagers do when he was not allowed to come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, after that, when again they addressed an ultimatum over the loud speaker, and said that if we did not surrender they would start shelling, we evacuated the civilians and, half an hour later, that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you evacuated from the village -- after the village was evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling started by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, the other members who were there also withdrew. I stayed on in the village. HVO members entered the village and captured me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know they were HVO members who captured you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who captured me did not have any insignia -- at least I did not notice any -- but, while they were taking me in, I saw some members with insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of uniform were they attired in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniform. They were well equipped -- they had automatic weapons, Motorolas and handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what happened after you were captured by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was captured, the members who captured me started to mistreat me. They hit me twice with rifle butts in the head and injured me. Afterwards, they tied my hands behind my back and they led me in the direction of the school at Bare. On the way they also mistreated me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were arrested, did you hear a conversation on the Motorola between the HVO soldiers and some others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. An HVO member had this Motorola in his hand, and he was guiding the shells towards the neighbouring village with it and, just then, a shell fell near us. He started cursing his own people, telling them to drop those shells a little further away and not so close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were taken to a school building after your arrest, to a building in Bare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the way to the school building, were you mistreated by anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. HVO members, on the way from the village to the school, mistreated me. They hit me with rifle butts, mostly in the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at any point in time were you ordered to take off your boots by the members of the HVO who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was near a stream -- they ordered to take off my boots, which they threw away, and I had to cross the stream twice, to the other bank and back twice. Then they took me in front of the school at Bare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were taken to the school building in Bare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They handed me over to their commander. I do not exactly recall his name, but I think it was Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you at or near the school building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly how much time I spent there, but I was there, and from there, I was transferred by bus to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Busovaca were you brought to by bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the bus station in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody escort you when you were brought by bus to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an HVO member and the driver, who was driving the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were brought to the bus station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken in front of a cafe bar and I was told to wait. After a short while, the same HVO member came and he took me again to the bus station. Actually, the cafe bar was at the station, too. It was all nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there, were you taken anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the bus station in Busovaca I was taken to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to this court what happened upon arrival in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Kaonik, I was admitted by someone -- I think his name was Marko Krilic, who wrote down my name in a book. He took off the handcuffs I had, and he took me and he drove me to the outpatients' clinic in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you driven to the outpatients' clinic in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They cleaned my wounds, they bandaged them, and then they took me back to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall to which building in Kaonik camp you were brought to -- what type of building was it that you were brought into in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It used to be a hangar of the former Yugoslav army and that is where the prison had been made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before being taken to the clinic, were you brought -- is it the same building that you were taken to upon arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be shown an aerial photograph of the camp, which has already been produced in evidence -- there are five copies. Could the usher please place the photograph on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the photograph on the projector and, with the pointer, show the building to which you were brought to in the Kaonik camp on that day? Could you please show it on the picture that is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please circle that building using a highlighter that is on the table and mark it with the letter "A".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were first brought to that building in the Kaonik camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it from that building that Marko Krilic took you to the outpatients' department or outpatients' clinic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to which building were you returned after being treated at the outpatients' clinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in that building were you put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of building was that -- was it a building --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a building, as I already said, where the hangar was, and that is where the prison was built, with cells, for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you put into a cell in that building after you were brought back from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which cell you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, number 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were put into that cell, where there already other prisoners in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I believe it was about 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to which ethnic group those other prisoners belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were put into that cell, were you taken out on labour detachments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly, but I believe it was the following day -- the 28th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Podjele.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you selected to be taken to Podjele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, we were all brought out of the cells into the hallway, and Marko Krilic was there calling out, and 20 of us went to Podjele to dig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to this court what happened at Podjele when you were taken there to dig?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to the Lasva River to dig some trenches there in the morning around 8 o'clock. We were guarded by the HVO members, one of whose name was Zare -- I believe he was the commander of this group. We were not allowed to sit down and rest. We asked for water and they gave us water from the Lasva River. This went on throughout the day until around 8 o'clock in the evening, when another group of the HVO members arrived, who were more decent than the previous ones. They allowed us to sit down and rest, to light up a cigarette in case we smoked, and then, later, around 10 o'clock, they took us to the village of Podjele itself, and there they gave us some food to eat. We continued to dig, with some breaks in between, until 11 o'clock the following morning. At 11 o'clock another group of prisoners arrived, it was the same number as we, and we went back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I have permission to show to the witness a map of the area? This map, too, has already been produced in evidence. I am submitting five copies for your Honours as well as to learned counsel for the Defence. (Handed). May that be assigned the next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you have said that you were taken to Podjele the next day. Could you please, looking at the map that is on the ELMO, and using one of the markers, highlight the area that you were taken to for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were brought back to the camp the next morning; where in the camp were you brought back to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly -- I believe it was cell number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other occasions on which you were taken for trench digging whilst you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken to next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prosje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day was it when you were taken to Prosje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was in the morning -- some time around 8 o'clock, and until about 10 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the selection process on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see it was similar like the first time -- we all came out in the hallway and Marko Krilic was calling people out. Whoever was called out stepped outside and then we were taken in trucks from the camp to the location where we were supposed to dig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken elsewhere for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Milavice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the time you were taken to Prosje, how many days thereafter were you taken to Milavice -- how many days after were you taken to Milavice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were taken to Milavice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the same process of selection of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig in Milavice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same -- let us say from 8 o'clock in the morning until dusk -- I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was Marko Krilic who called out the names of the prisoners. Do you know what his role was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing -- do you remember what kind of attire he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have any insignia on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you in the camp, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 27 January until 8 February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was on 8 February that you were released from detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an exchange and I went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many prisoners were exchanged on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the number, but I believe it was about 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said after your release you went to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there, did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Zenica, I went back to my family again, and I joined the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After joining the BiH army, where were you posted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a village that is adjacent to my village -- no, no, no -- I was assigned to Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when fighting broke out in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 16 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that day between whom did the fighting break out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the members of the army and the members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when fighting broke out in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croat Defence Council forces attacked with all their might, my village -- the place where I was staying. At one point six of us, a group of six, were in a forest where we were patrolling. We spent the entire day there, and some time close to the end of the day a colleague of mine and I fell asleep, and again the HVO members came and took the two of us prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you and a colleague of yours were taken prisoner. Your Honours, the Prosecution intends to call the colleague who was taken prisoner with him, and, in respect of that witness, the Prosecution intends to make a similar application for protective measures. Therefore, I do not want the witness to come out with the name of that colleague. Instead, your Honours, I am tendering to the witness a sheet of paper with the colleague's name on it so the witness can confirm whether it is the same person with whom -- whether that person was arrested together with him. May the usher be please asked to show the sheet of paper to the witness to confirm whether the name appearing on that sheet is that of his colleague? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, it may be shown to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I do tender that as an exhibit under seal. Witness, you said that you and your colleague, whose name you confirmed as that which appeared on the sheet of paper, were arrested by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, after being arrested, where were you all taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were arrested at a place called Pecine, we were taken to Zabrde. After Zabrde, after that we were taken to the school in Gornja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in the school in Gornja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about two nights, and the members of the Croat Defence Council were coming there. They mistreated us, and they shot over our heads. We slept on the concrete, we had nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken to thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I believe it was two or three days later, the HVO members arrived again. They blindfolded us and tied our hands behind our backs with a wire, and they took us out. In the meantime, one of the two of us asked them where they were taking us, and one of the members told us that we were being taken to be executed. They placed us on a tractor, and they drove us across some hills -- at least that was the sensation that we had. Since we were blindfolded and we could not see, they brought us to some village where we could hear voices of women and children, and they transferred us to a trunk of a small passenger vehicle. After a short period of time, we were again transported -- I believe this was a van or a bus, but I am not sure of it. We were brought to a location which I had never seen before. They took the blindfolds off -- there were five or six soldiers present who had stockings over their faces. They untied our hands there, and they put us in some kind of a manhole, which was about five metres deep. We climbed downstairs into it -- it was some kind of either a water main or sewers with some vents. We were there from the moment we were brought there until it got dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend the night in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, what is the relevance of all this evidence -- does it bear on the charges at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I am seeking to elicit from the witness -- from here onwards he was taken to Kaonik camp where he was detained and subject to mistreatment. So, were you taken out of the manhole at any point in time that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as we reached that spot, when they took off the blindfolds, and untied our hands, they put us in this manhole, and, just before dark fell, an HVO soldier came -- a fair young man, who called us to come out -- we did. He offered us some food. As it was cold in the manhole, we could not eat -- we were shivering -- our hands were shaking, so we asked him if he could give us a blanket to warm ourselves. He said he would see, and he left. A short while later, he came back and told us to come out again and he took us to a container, where there were blankets -- quite a lot of them -- and there were lunch packets -- packed lunches there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent the night in the container, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told us to clean it up a bit, because the blankets were thrown all over the place, and to sleep there. That is what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning, the same soldier, HVO soldier, came and took us to the same manhole, and shut us up there. We spent some time there -- I do not recall exactly how long -- and then he came back again, called out one of us. As my colleague was the first, he went out. I waited inside -- I was locked up there. He was taken away for interrogation. When my colleague returned, they took me. This lasted about half an hour. I came back. A little later again, they came to fetch us again, and they took us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to some kind of a mobile armoured vehicle -- a vehicle, like a transporter. We were escorted by the military police, and they transported us to the Busovaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were escorted by the military police. The military police of which army escorted you to the Busovaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police that escorted us to the Busovaca camp belonged to the army of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the "Busovaca camp", you mean the Kaonik camp to which you were earlier brought to and from which you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell this court what happened upon arrival in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since they had transported us in this vehicle to the Kaonik camp, we came out at the entrance gates, and, from there, we went on, on foot, to the actual prison building, where, in front of the door, the commander of the prison was waiting -- Zlatko Aleksovski -- with several more guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commander of the prison say anything when you entered the camp building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he introduced himself as the camp commander. He ordered them to take off what we had, if we had parts of camouflage uniforms, and the laces of our boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were put up in cell number 6. We were there for a while when members of the HVO military police came. Their names were Zarko and Miro. They started mistreating us -- that is me and my colleague. We were lying on the pallets. They jumped on the pallets and started hitting us, and kicking us in the back, in the kidney area, and in the head. This went on for some time. They apparently seemed to have tired and they said they would go and have a rest and that they would be back. They did come back -- the same two men, Miro and Zarko. Miro started hitting my colleague, and Zarko stood by watching. At that moment, the prison commander came, Zlatko Aleksovski and he told Zarko, "What are you waiting for? Why do you not act in the same way as Miro?" And he obeyed and Zarko also started hitting me. This ended. Afterwards, some HVO members -- they were also in the prison I think -- and they brought us lunch, or dinner, whatever it was -- anyway, it was some food. Then again Zarko and Miro came in, who threw these beans into our face. It was still warm -- I mean the food -- and then they started mistreating us again. My colleague fainted at one point and I shook him, fearing that he was dead. But he came to. After that, someone came in -- I think he, too, was an HVO member, who was there in the prison -- not captured but he was there. His name was Goran Medugorac. I know that previously he was in Zenica and he was a member of the HOS. He started mistreating me, and he was saying that I had allegedly mistreated him earlier on during a dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the mistreatment that you had to undergo this time at the hands of Goran Medugorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was physical mistreatment; beating, blows mainly in the kidney area, and at the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as alleged by Goran Medugorac, do you remember mistreating him elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had never even seen him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what happened to you in the camp thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, Anto Cakic came, who ordered me -- as I was beaten up, I had to lie down. Anto Cakic ordered me to stand at attention. He would come in every 15 minutes to check whether I was still standing, and, when he came, he would occasionally hit me with his leg or with his fist, and this went on like this until some time around 10 o'clock in the evening, when this same Anto went off somewhere, and I did not see him again until somewhere before the end when I was about to be exchanged. I learned later that he had gone to the front some place, and that he had been wounded there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, whilst you were detained in the camp, were you taken out of the camp on labour detachment -- I am referring to your second stint of detention in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After all of this, the very next day, we were taken to dig at a location called Strane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the map before you, could you mark the location Strane with the highlighter that you have beside you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also, earlier on in the course of your testimony, said, referring in the course of your first period of detention, that you were taken to dig trenches in Prosje and again in Milavice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark those places on the map that is before you, Exhibit 81?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that place that you marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of the place that you marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milavice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also mark Prosje on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have marked Prosje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think you have marked Podjele, Milavice and then Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prosje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You said you were taken to Strane; about how many prisoners were taken to Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you have to do in Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to dig large trenches for an anti-aircraft gun which was on a truck -- a small TAM vehicle. While we were digging, HVO members guarded us with automatic rifles, while later -- I do not know what time it was exactly, because we left at 8 in the morning and perhaps around noon -- lunch came. HVO members who brought the lunch started to mistreat the prisoners, especially those who were wearing, shall we say, camouflage parts of uniforms -- anything in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated by the HVO members on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was not, but, when the digging was over, as all I had on me was my underwear and long pants, they ordered me and another colleague to climb up out of the trench and to tread on the earth that we had dug out. A sniper on the side of the army was shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "the army", which army do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BiH army. We were stamping on this earth -- luckily, we were not hit, but bullets were whizzing past us. When we finished it all, on the way back towards the truck, we had to carry with us to the truck the casings of the anti-aircraft gun, which they were collecting and I do not know for what reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you engaged in digging in Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in the morning -- I think from about 8 until just before darkness fell. As I had been beaten up, I could not really dig -- I just had to shovel the earth. I could not bend down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were you brought back to the camp that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That evening I was taken to the camp, again to cell number 6. When we got there, my colleague and I, the cell was bloodstained. We saw that somebody had been there while we had been away. We lay down. A short while later another two prisoners appeared escorted by the guards. They came in. They were also bloodstained. They were also mistreated in our cell while we had been away digging and they stayed with us. When they closed the door and left, we were able to ask them what had happened and they told us that, before, they had been in the hangar. They were taken to dig that same day, like us, and both of them were wounded there -- one in the back and the other in the arm, but later I learned the name of one of the two of these two prisoners and it was Omer Lugonjic, and I cannot recall the name of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I will take a few more minutes. Will I proceed or would your Honours be inclined to take a break and reconvene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that we should have a break to give the witness a rest, and we, too, need a break -- all of us -- so we are going to have a 20 minute break now. (10.26am) (A short break) (10.55am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. Witness, before the recess you described to this court your experiences whilst trench digging in Strane and what you observed after returning from trench digging -- what you observed in the camp. Were you taken elsewhere for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken -- I do not know exactly, but, in any event, we were taken to Kula, Loncari, Polom -- those were the places -- Popece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit P80, could you please, using a highlighter, mark those places that you have just mentioned on the map that is before you, the map that has been marked P80 -- I think that is P79 -- sorry, P81. Looking at P81, could you please mark those places that you just mentioned -- those places that you were taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you mark them, could you say what those places are? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Carica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Loncari, Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, using the same marker, may I ask you to mark those places that you circled on the map -- you have marked Prosje, a place you were taken for trench digging during your first period of detention in the camp; could you mark Prosje with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Milavice, also during your first period of detention, with the letter "C"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then during your second period of detention, you were taken to Strane; could you mark Strane with the letter "D"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Carica with the letter "E"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Loncari which you marked a while ago with the letter "F" and Kula which you marked last with the letter "G"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were taken to Carica. Do you remember you being maltreated whilst you were trench digging in Carica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken to Carica on several occasions. I cannot remember exactly -- in fact, Carica and Kula I was taken several times -- to the other places only once, and I was abused there by members of the Croat Defence Council, and it was one person and his name was Anto Condra. He beat me and mistreated me, and, later -- I did not say that in my statement, but he would come to the prison afterwards inebriated and besides me, he mistreated other inmates who were in the cell. This happened in cell number 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than these places that you marked in the map, were you also taken to Polom on any occasion for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called the Polom, not Prolum, but, yes, I was. This was at Carica location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that the time you were taken to Carica that you were also taken to Polom, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, every time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now on those places that you were taken to, were any of those places on the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, Podjele, where I dug, was not on the front-line. At Strane, it was the front-line. At Polom, also; at Kula I dug also at the front-line, and beside the front-line, it was also -- I do not know what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the map that is before you, could you also mark the area of Polom that you just mentioned where you had to dig on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause). (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you mark that with the letter "H"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you also remember what the conditions in the camp were like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe those conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, as far as the conditions in the camp are concerned, I consider them very bad. We could go out to the toilet -- we had to knock on the door and announce the number of the cell. When we would say this, the guard would come, who was on duty -- he would open the door -- and we had to be very quick. We were given a very short period of time and we had to come back fast. The toilet was within the prison. I never had a shower throughout this period. The food was horrible and I also want to say that anybody could come of the HVO members at any time and could abuse anyone that he was looking for down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have heating inside the cell in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have sleeping facilities inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was something called pallets. There were some wooden boards and, on top of them, there were some blankets -- somewhere, there were no blankets, and there were blankets with which we covered ourselves -- I had one and almost everybody did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those occasions, witness, when you were taken out for -- when you and the others were taken out for trench digging, is it that -- what was the procedure for selection during your second period of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The procedure of taking prisoners to dig, that is, to forced labour, was as follows: Marko Krilic would read out the list; we were in the cells, and, when he would read out my name, I would say the number of the cell, the guards would open the door, and we would step outside into the hallway and that is where we lined up and then we were transported in the trucks to the location where we were to dig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in the course of your testimony this morning you also referred to your colleague, and I showed you a sheet of paper with the name of your colleague written on it. Is it the same person that you referred to as your colleague throughout your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember until when you were detained in Kaonik camp for the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 19 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the circumstances under which you were released from prison on 19 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an exchange took place. I do not know how it came about, but at any rate an exchange took place, and we were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether any organisation was involved in the exchange or in the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed that it was the Red Cross, because they came to visit us while we were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be shown Prosecution exhibit number 80. I have just a few more questions of the witness. That was the aerial photograph of the camp, your Honours. (Handed). Witness, you have marked on that aerial photograph, Prosecution exhibit number 80, the building that you have circled with the letter "A" and that is the building where you said that you were first detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your second spell of detention, could you show on this map in which building you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same building -- can I mark it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed to mark that building. It is the same building that you already marked as "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when you were brought to that building on the second occasion in April 1993, upon arrival, the camp commander introduced himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look around this court and say whether that camp commander is present in this court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, will you please give us the -- that he looked in the direction of the accused, Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, is he the same camp commander that ordered Zarko to do the same thing as Miro as when you and your colleague were being beaten and abused in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness L, we have every respect for your suffering and the pain you went through, but you will now be answering questions that Mr. Mikulicic may be asking you under the same solemn oath. Mr. Mikulicic or Mr. Joka? Cross-examined by MR. JOKA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. L, I am Mr. Joka, attorney representing Zlatko Aleksovski. I will ask you a number of questions. First, by way of introduction, what is your formal education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not completed any school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But which school did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary school and now I am attending part-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four grades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, eight grades of elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you speak any foreign language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not ask you anything about your first stay at the Kaonik camp but only your second. Could you tell us with greater precision when you went to Kaonik for the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, because I cannot remember, but I think it was around 19 or 20 April until 19 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In that context, can you tell the court -- I am talking about your second stay at Kaonik -- when were you registered by any international organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it at the beginning of your stay, the middle or towards the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you for sure, but I think it was about 15 days after I arrived at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us how you were captured and accommodated in Gornja Veceriska and you were there mistreated by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or your colleague -- the person whose name we are not mentioning, so I will continue calling him your colleague -- were you or your colleague injured in any way on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. These were light injuries -- bruises on the head and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what were they from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of blows -- with the hand, with a fist, with the palm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a fist, with a fist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you hit in the eyes, the mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here (indicates), on the cheek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, later on, when you were in the manholes that you described to us, the storage space with the pipes and vents, was anyone there mistreated -- you or your colleague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my colleague was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that somebody beat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not see that, but, judging by what he told me, he was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was beaten by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By an HVO member, whom I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You are back in Kaonik now. Who were you with in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The moment we arrived and until the next day in the evening, the two of us were alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or your colleague provoke any kind of incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the event with the two members of the HVO police, Zarko and Miro, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We learnt later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard them calling each other by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know those people from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned somebody called Medugorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us his name and first name. You said that you had never seen the man before. How do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know his name -- I learnt his name after all of this, maybe a month later -- he took me out asking me to wash his underwear and the clothing he was wearing, and, while I was washing it he sat there, and he spoke about himself, what he had done, where he had been and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you learned from him why he was in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he just told me that he had been in Zenica and he had done something. After all that, the two of us -- it is rather strange -- but we somehow got close -- we became kind of friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, you said that there were other Croats at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know that Micic was there -- I do not remember his first name -- he was also sitting there as you put it -- he was from Kakanj -- there was someone called Mladen. There was another HOS member from Zenica whose name was Dzemo who was also there in detention, in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the attitude of those people in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In most cases, they treated me correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other prisoners, the other Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about the others -- they will probably be able to tell you best. I can only speak on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. How did they treat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said at the beginning, as far as Medugorac is concerned -- no, I am thinking about the others -- he treated us -- his attitude towards us was such that he would mistreat us, the Muslim prisoners who were there -- he did not mistreat me, though. I cannot say that he did. The others did not mistreat me, either -- I cannot say they did when they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dzemo's ethnic group is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was a Muslim, most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber about the incident with the -- a man called Anto Cakic. Do you know who Cakic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Cakic from before. I knew him from prison and I still know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the municipality of Busovaca and Busovaca is not far, so we would see each other in Busovaca and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Cakic know that you were at Kaonik for a second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this subject discussed between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At least, in my opinion, that was the reason why he mistreated me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please explain yourself to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not aware of my first stay, but he must have learnt about it from somebody else, that I was there for a second time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I did not understand you. Why would he mistreat you -- just because you were there for a second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When talking about Cakic, you said he did not come that evening because he had to go to the front. What about the other guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly how many guards there were that night, but all the guards went somewhere -- there was just one left, whose name I do not know. That is it. Afterwards, I learnt, when Anto Cakic came back, that he had been wounded that night when he went somewhere and that is why he was not in the prison for a certain period of time. I cannot remember for how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, that that night there was only one guard left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to a different issue. Were there other people at Kaonik apart from this Cakic, who knew that you were there for a second time, either neighbours or guards, or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know. A moment ago you were telling the court about the conditions in prison and you said that the food was poor. Was it cold or cooked food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see. There were periods when we had cooked food and other periods when we had cold food. The food was terrible, especially when the conflicts were on between the HVO and the BiH army, then the food was the worst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it at its best?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were times when the food was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what you mean when you say "good" or "bad" food when you are talking about Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us, everything was good, whatever food we were given. The two of us would eat from one plate with a slice of bread each, and there was a soup with a couple of macaroni inside. This was served twice a day, and then I do not remember when this was exactly when we would get somewhat better food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there beans -- were there beans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned heating, that there was no heating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there heating anywhere else in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a stove, but it was not sufficient to heat the whole prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the stove burning during the winter, that is, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the commander's office was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a stove of his own inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a believer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the possibility to pray?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who prevented you from doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody prevented me -- we did not ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the ethnic composition of the village was before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all Muslims in the village -- there was just one Croat home with an elderly woman living there. She left before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any incidents with that single house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that somebody removed the cross from that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think the old woman died before the conflict actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the village of Pezici is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in the same area we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in that village of Pezici during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the military sense, was there a conflict between HVO units and the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, HVO units attacked -- now we are going back to 27 January, they attacked our village and the next day they attacked the village of Pezici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did events develop in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in Pezici at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, do you have any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no questions in re-examination, except that I would wish to move for a redaction of an answer that went down in cross-examination. The answer is on page 45 of the transcript, line 3, where there is a reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay, you are right. Please show it to Mr. Joka. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness L, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In connection with the conditions in the Kaonik camp, you said that all the HVO members could come in whenever they wanted and mistreat the detainees -- did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Who were these HVO members -- were they working in the camp, or did they come -- were they soldiers, were they guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were mostly people coming in a drunken state and they could enter the cells whenever they wanted -- at least, in my cell. I do not know about the other cells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness L. We wish to thank you for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, the next witness, who is referred to in the motion of the Prosecutor in paragraph 4 -- the fourth witness that appears in paragraph number 4, if your Honours please, on page 3 of that motion of 20 March 1998, has sought also measures for the protection of his name and identity, and we have given that information to Mr. Mikulicic and, as I understand, there is no objection to that. We would ask that the image of his face be distorted in a similar way to the last witness, and that he be given the pseudonym "Witness M", if your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, is that all right with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is fine -- the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In that event, I call Witness M as our next witness, your Honour. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please, pull your chair up closer to the microphone, thank you. You are going to answer questions that the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, is going to address to you. WITNESS M Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, their Honours have granted you certain protections with respect to your identity, so, throughout the course of your examination, I will be referring to you as "Witness M", do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For that reason, you should not give your name during the course of your evidence in answer to a question. Would you look for me for the moment at Exhibit 82, please? Would you just open this piece of paper -- look at the name that is contained there and can you tell me whether or not that is your name (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that might be shown to Mr. Mikulicic. Witness, would you look at the piece of paper that I am now showing you and can you tell me whether or not the name of the village that you resided in prior to the war in January 1993 is written on that sheet of paper? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, and might it be tendered under seal? Witness M, what is your ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, I omitted to wait for that. Witness, what is your ethnic background, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your age?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the early part of 1993 -- and when I speak of the early part of 1993, I am talking of January of that year -- were you in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a soldier in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you engaged -- you were on military duty, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was engaged in the municipality of Travnik near -- the town of Travnik on the front-lines against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Chetniks", who do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb and Montenegrin aggressors who attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, from time to time, when you were off military duty, return to your village during that year, the early part of that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, apart from the Serb and Montenegrin forces that you were fighting, was there any other unrest in the area at the time that developed during early January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the territory of the municipality where I lived, there were a few incidents with the Croat Defence Council, and the tensions spread on 26 and 27 January, and at that time I was at the front-line, as I said before, in the Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these tensions developed between the Croats and -- had this been expected or anticipated by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never expected it personally, neither did the people in my village, because we had good co-existence with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the predominant ethnic group in your village -- the Muslims or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke of 26 and 27 January 1993. What in fact occurred?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then later, in the month, travel back to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I came to my village on 2 February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back, what did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back, I saw that the village was laid to waste -- in one part of the village all the inhabitants had fled to neighbouring village and in another there were a few villagers left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined in the defence of my village -- the defence was organised -- for future developments. I was assigned to the front-line against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, now you became involved in the conflict with the Croat forces; is that right, as opposed to the Serb/Montenegrin forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did you play in this? What were you to do? What were your military duties in relation to this -- what were you required to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a regular soldier, who was assigned to the front-line, but, during this period, after I had come back to the village, some kind of a truce was signed between the BiH army forces and the HVO forces, which lasted until that second conflict which started on 16 April 1993, so that there were no particular conflicts in the village in this intervening period from when I returned to the village until 16 April when the new conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, on 16 April, where were you specifically on that time -- at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assigned to a village watch -- a village guard in the village that was again neighbouring my own village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, somewhere around 6 o'clock in the morning, the shelling started on the part of the HVO -- the shelling of the village where I was on guard duty, and a neighbouring village which, until that time, had not been attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what transpired as a result of this shelling and this attack that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- we knew that we were attacked by the HVO, but that was the only thing that was clear at that point. We did not know anything else -- why and how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on in the morning, say at about 11 or near to midday, were you captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because, from that position, you could see the village. I saw my village burning -- houses there, on fire and, at that moment, an HVO unit appeared, which took us prisoner -- myself and a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken prisoner, did you notice the way your captors -- the people that took you into captivity, did you notice how they were dressed, the soldiers, and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing camouflage uniforms with visible HVO insignia on the left sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at Exhibit 79, please? Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness to receive the exhibit, I might ask for a redaction on page 52, lines 12 to 13. I think it has already been shown to your Honours. Just looking at this piece of paper that you are now being shown, witness, there is a name that appears there. Was that person with you at the time that you were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken when you were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to a nearby weekend house settlement -- a place called Zabrde. That is where we were tied up by the HVO soldiers. We had to put our hands behind our backs. They tied us up with wire, and then they bound us together with wire and then we were taken to a village of Gornja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Gornja Veceriska, where did they place you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in Gornja Veceriska that day -- we spent the night there, and the next day. They tied us up, they blindfolded us with some fabric, and we were taken to Kace near Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Kace, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Kace, we were placed in a some kind of a manhole -- I do not know what purpose it served for -- I know it was very cold and there was a strong stench coming from it. After we were placed in this manhole, my colleague and I were taken out, one by one, and taken to a structure nearby, where the HVO forces were accommodated, and I was beaten up in the office of their security officer by an unknown man. I had my back turned to him when he started beating me, so that I was not able to see his face, nor would I be able to identify him. I was beaten up, and then they asked of me to give a statement, and what they were interested in was what kind of forces we had, even though at that time I did not know what kind of forces the BiH army had, and then, after that, he told me that a decision was taken that myself and my colleague would be executed, and he asked me whether I had any family in Zenica or Travnik so that they would be notified after we were executed so that the location of our execution would be passed to the next of kin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back just a little bit, from the time that you were captured through to this moment when you were told that you were to be executed, had you been beaten at any stage, other than the incident that you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were beaten on that other occasion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was beaten. The first time we were beaten up there in the school in Gornja Veceriska, we were in the hallway there of that school. They gave us some card boards, so we could lie down and rest -- it was on a concrete floor, and we were beaten up there; we were mistreated by both the civilians and the soldiers who were there. We stayed the night there in Gornja Veceriska and the next day a group of 10 soldiers came, and we were beaten there and we were beaten up pretty heavily.
