utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were beaten on these occasions, did at any stage you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lost consciousness at Veceriska, but they would again beat me back into consciousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you had been told that you would be executed, what happened next -- what was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me back to the manhole, and then my colleague was taken out also to give a statement, and after he returned back to where I was, he was also told that we would be executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you spend another night in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in the manhole until the dusk and then a guard who was there -- I do not know whether it was on his own initiative or under someone's orders, but I think it was just his good intentions -- he took us out of the manhole and placed us in a container which was near the manhole, and then again early in the morning, before it dawned, we were transferred back into the manhole and, as the guard said, for his own security's sake, because as he said, he was not allowed to take us out of the manhole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next morning, after you had been put back into the manhole, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were put back into the manhole and we spent about three or four hours there, and then we were again called out, we came outside, and two HVO military policemen were waiting there for us, and further down in front of the building, I saw a group of their soldiers, of whom I thought they were the firing squad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and the colleague that you have identified when you looked at Exhibit 79 say anything to each other in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would tell my colleague while we were still in the manhole, and not knowing what would happen, we were somehow sure that they would kill us, but I would say to him that there was a possibility that we might be massacred -- mutilated -- before being killed, so I said to him, "If they do start to mutilate us and torture us, let us try and escape, so let them kill us with rifle shots". We agreed to behave in that way and that is exactly what we would have done, I am sure, if they had started to torture us and mutilate us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But instead of doing this, what happened -- instead of them doing that to you, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we reached this group of soldiers, who were in front of the building where I had been the day before, two soldiers, or two military policemen stepped out -- one of them, I learned that his name was Zlatko Nakic and they told us to get into the bus. The bus had the Red Cross sign on it. We entered the bus, and the driver was already there inside, and we asked him where we were going. He told us, "You are going to Kaonik". I felt relief, because I had assumed -- or, rather, I knew that there was a camp there, but I also knew that there were civilians there, so there was a greater chance that I would stay alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This colleague that you were with, whom you identified when you looked at Exhibit 79, had he been to Kaonik before, so far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had already spent some time there during the conflict in his village. He had been captured, and taken to the Kaonik camp, and he had spent there, I think, about 15 days, the first time he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been to the Kaonik camp during the course of that year, 1993, when it was used as a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been there before like your colleague, to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, this was to be your first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Kaonik, tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived at Kaonik under armed escort, from the place we got off the bus, and then we reached the building where we were put up. We were met there by a group of guards and the director of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know this person was the director of the camp, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know straight away, but, after entering the cell, my colleague told me who was who, because he knew, as he had been there before, and he already knew the persons who met us, so that I learnt the name then, and who was in charge of the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you learn then was in charge of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the man who was in charge -- everybody called him "director" -- Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see how he was dressed on the first occasion that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing a camouflage uniform with HVO insignia on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say or do anything when you first arrived at the camp on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really remember. I remember that he laughed, that he was making some sort of jokes at our expense, but we were mistreated there by one of the guards, and Mr. Aleksovski was present throughout that time while we were searched and taken to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing they did to us, we had already been searched 10 or 15 times -- I cannot remember exactly -- wherever we went, we were searched, though we had nothing on us; everything was taken away. All I had were some gloves when I reached Kaonik. They took away those gloves, too, and the guard who was harassing us, he told us to turn around to face him, to look straight ahead, or, rather, sideways, so that he could point his gun at our noses, as he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, they took us to cell number 6 of this building where the cells were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at this photograph that I now show you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, excuse me for interrupting you, but I think it is time for a 15-minute break, if you do not mind; I hope it does not upset your questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we will have a 15-minute break. (12.08pm) (A short break) (12.30pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, before we go on, through my fault, I may have been misleading when I spoke of the village that you lived at. I just ask you to look at this sheet of paper, if you would, for me. I think precisely is this the village where you live? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that under seal and perhaps it could be shown to Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to clear up that matter, witness, the other village that I showed you on the other slip of paper, that is a neighbouring village, is it, where the attack first commenced in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are at the part of your evidence where you said you were taken into cell number 6 in the building when you first arrived and I was about to show you a photograph and would you look at this photograph for me, please, and see if you can identify it? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness M, I want you to look at this photograph for me, please, and can you tell me whether it looks familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pick up a coloured pen there on the side of the projector? Can you mark the place where you first arrived -- when you first arrived at the Kaonik camp where you alighted from your bus, are you able to mark that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you put for me the letter "A" there, please -- not "E" but "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there where did you go? Using the red marker, can you colour the direction that you went from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with the letter "B" can you put a mark at the place where you say you went inside into cell number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, when you first arrived at the camp in April 1993, can you tell us which building the office of the commander was, Mr. Aleksovski, was it in building A or building B when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in building B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did his office later change to another place during the time that you were at the camp, or was it always at B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was here, but the prisoners who were in the camp made a new office for him at the entrance to building B. It was not moved to another building -- it was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you were put into the cell, what did you see; what was the first thing you saw -- can you describe the interior of the cell for us, that is, cell number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the cell, there were pallets and, to the left, as we entered, there was like a straw mattress and the guard who brought us there told us that we could not lie on that straw mattress, but to the right on the boards, the wooden boards, the pallets that had been made there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say any reason why you could not lie on it, or he just made that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not give any reason. He just told us that, and we knew that we could not, so we sat in the part where there was no straw -- there was just a blanket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that night when you were in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night one of the guards came in -- his name was Anto Cakic. He entered and he ordered us to stand in one corner, one of us in one corner and the other one in the other, so I went to the left-hand corner of the cell, and my colleague went to the right-hand corner, and he said he would be back, and he left the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know this person was called Anto Cakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, because my colleague, when he was there for the first time, had met him, and before the war broke out on the territory of the municipality, I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he told you to do this, to stand in either corner of the cell, what was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, he came back in, and he started beating my colleague, and he started bleeding from the nose from the beating, and then he told him to go and wash his nose in the toilet, which was in the building. While my colleague was walking out, he approached me and he hit me on the left side of my face. He asked me where I was from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he hit you with on the side of your face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With his fist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he hit you with a full fist, or did he hit you hard, or was it just a light blow -- can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a hard blow, because I started bleeding from the mouth from the blow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me where I was from and what my father's name was. I told him my father's name and where I was from. He then said that he knew my father, that he had been an acquaintance of his before the war had broken out, and he told me that I could lie down and go to sleep, whereas he would beat my colleague all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that, that he would be beaten all night, your colleague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Niemann, but I think we have a minor technical problem -- I have just been informed -- regarding the French translation. Perhaps we need to stop for about five minutes to try and deal with the problem. Will five minutes be enough? We will rise for five minutes. (12.44pm) (A short break) (12.50pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I think the technical problem has been resolved, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness M, did you then do as the guard had said and that is lay down on the pallet and go to sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him whether I could go to the toilet. He said I could, so I went to the toilet, and, when I came back, I did what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was very tired, because it was the third day that we had not slept properly, I just heard them come in once to beat my colleague. I fell asleep and, in the morning, I woke up, I saw my colleague lying next to me. I asked him what had happened. He told me that they had beaten him that night, until some time before dawn, and this was visible on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say your "colleague", that is the person whom you identified earlier when I showed you that name, Exhibit 79?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then, after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that first night in the Kaonik camp, the next day Mr. Aleksovski came with five or six HVO soldiers and they entered our cell. Mr. Aleksovski told them, addressing the soldiers, he said, "These are the men from the place where I come from".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He used the name -- at least part of the name of the place where you came from, is that right, which has been tendered now as Exhibit 84?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Then two soldiers came up to me and started beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers that were with Mr. Aleksovski and who started to beat you, did you understand them to be guards or were they regular HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not think that they were guards, I thought that they were regular HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they in fact beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski stay there, or did he go away when they started to beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there -- he was present when they started to beat me and they beat me so badly that I did not even notice where Mr. Aleksovski was, but my colleague told me that he was there all the time, standing at the door and laughing while they were beating me and that, later on, he told another two HVO soldiers to beat my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he told" them that, are you referring to Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they beat you with, and what did they beat your colleague with, these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the soldiers, who was beating me, had a police truncheon. His name is Ivca Kristo. I do not know the other one's name. This Ivca beat me with this truncheon and with his feet, whereas the other one kicked me, beat me with his fists, in any way he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retain your consciousness throughout this beating, or did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first beating, I was still conscious, but, when they went out the first time, Ivca addressed us and said that they would beat us every half hour. I do not know whether half an hour went by, but they came back after that and they beat us again. That day they beat us six times while we were in cell number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Aleksovski at any other time during the course of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Mr. Aleksovski say anything to the guards other than what you have said, that "these are from the village" -- your village -- apart from him saying that, did he say anything else to the guards that you can remember during the course of your beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard them saying in the corridor, when they went out for the first time, when they were walking through the door, that he told them that there would be a party in cell number 6 during that day. The party, I assume, implied that we would be beaten, and this came true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other word used during the time that you were at the camp to describe people being beaten -- was there any other word that was used from time to time that you can remember now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that, while they were beating me, they were saying it was a "dance party".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "dancing", what did you understand by that -- what were they doing when they were so-called "dancing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This word, a "dance", we understood to mean mistreatment, beatings, and we proved to be right, as well as various kinds of provocations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were beaten about six times on that day. Was it always the same people that beat you, or did the people that beat you change at all, that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not always the same people who came. Ivca came that day three times. After that, some other unknown people came. I know that one of them came from the surroundings of Vitez, and he came just when they had brought us food in the cell. Before that, I had to go to the toilet and I did not dare go outside, nor did I dare ask anyone for permission, so I used the can that was in the cell, thinking that it was there for that purpose and I relieved myself in it. The guard, or one of the soldiers, had come in before that with the food. I went to relieve myself after that in this tin can that was in the cell and the man who had brought in the food came in again, and asked me where I had relieved myself. I told him, "Here" and he said, "Well, who told you to do that?"; I did not know what to say. Later, they told me that, after that, if you had to go to the toilet, but you could only go during meal time, and if you needed to go to the toilet, you could use these cans that were in the cell -- you were not allowed to knock on the door often to be let out and then the soldier who had asked me where I had urinated threw the food at me and started beating me again. He beat me so badly on that occasion that I lost consciousness. He would go out of the cell and then come back again. A second time when this soldier was beating me I asked him to kill me rather than torture me any longer and then he said, "It is easier to die like this". What he meant was that he would continue torturing me until I died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you urinated in the can, did you look at your urine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My urine -- I always had this urge to urinate and, in my urine there were visible traces of blood from the previous beating and from the current beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in pain in parts of your body when you had this beating -- did any particular part of your body feel in particular pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this second time, when the soldier beat me up in the cell, after this meal we did not eat, I was lying helplessly -- I could not feel anything in my legs; I was all numb, so was my back. After some time, I heard somebody talking on the door -- there was a dialogue going on between two people to the effect that, "They are alive or they are not alive" and then one of them said to the other, "Go and check and see if they are alive". He opened the cell, entered, and pulled me by my big toe. I just managed to move my head to the right so that his comment was, "Good, they are alive" and he went out after that. A little later, two others came in -- I know their names -- I met them in the camp -- Goran Medugorac and Micic Zoran, who were there in the camp as some kind of guards, or really they were under some sort of arrest -- that is what I gathered. They were HVO soldiers, and they came again to beat my colleague, saying that he had been beaten less and that they would make up for it so that he would catch up with me and then they beat him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed, this Zoran Micic and Goran Medugorac, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your condition, your physical condition like after these beatings, can you describe it for us? Were you bruised; did you have full use of your arms and legs -- can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this mistreatment the first day, I could not move at all. I had a visible scar on the left-hand side of my face -- I forgot this detail, while they were beating me, they were saying to one another that they not beat me on my face so that it would not be visible. However, one of them kicked me in the face with his boot, maybe by accident, and my face was -- my whole body was black and blue down to the ankles, and up to my neck -- there were visible bruises all over my body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you maintain the feeling in your limbs, in your arms and legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some kind of feeling remained, but after all that, after everything I suffered in the camp, I am not able to do things that I was able to do before and that concerns both my limbs, my spine -- I still have pain in the chest and back areas. This comes occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident a few days after you had been taken to the Kaonik camp, when you were taken out of your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what happened was Mr. Aleksovski and Mr. Marko Krilic, who was his deputy, came to get me and my colleague in our cell. They told us to get out and follow them and, in front of the building which I marked as "B", a TV crew of some sort was waiting. They did not introduce themselves to us; they did not say what TV they were from -- they spoke our language and we could understand them well. Mr. Aleksovski said, "Here is CNN to tape you" and one person from the TV crew approached us -- he was I guess the reporter, and he introduced -- identified us as the soldiers of the Muslim forces. I reacted to that, and I told him that we were not soldiers of the Muslim forces, but that we were soldiers of the Regular Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Krilic approached and said, "You are going to say what you are told to say. You are a member of the Muslim forces and that is how it is going to be". I said, "Very well" and again they started taping something. The reporter's questions were what were our names, where were we from, and then he asked us about the conditions of the place where we were. He asked us about the food, what the accommodation was like, whether we were being beaten, whether we were being mistreated and such details -- I did not know what to tell him. I wanted to tell him that the food was awful, that the conditions were terrible, but, while I was waiting to respond, Mr. Krilic approached me and said, "The conditions are fine, the food is fine, the accommodation is fine. Do not complain. You have nothing to think about". I said, "I did not know this until now, so fine" and then he also said, "When they ask you about the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia, you are going to say that the Muslims are responsible for all of that. They do not want to live together with the Croats, that you attacked them first" and things like that. That is what I said to this TV crew, which was taping us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the television stopped while you were told what to say by Mr. Krilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I hesitated about any answer, if I said anything that was not convenient for them, immediately the gentleman would say to stop taping and Mr. Krilic would come over and he would tell me what I was to say. That is, what they wanted me to say. Meanwhile, Mr. Aleksovski was two or three metres away from us and observing it and he would occasionally laugh and occasionally he would throw in remarks like, "You should feel honoured by having CNN taping you and visiting you". However, I could not see any logos or anything that would let me know this was CNN or international television. Later, from a Croat, I learned that it was a local TV crew from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the camp at Kaonik, were you ever visited by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Red Cross visited us on several occasions -- probably four or five times while I was in the Kaonik camp. They first came maybe 10 days after my capture and this includes the places where I was before arriving in Kaonik, so on 24 and 25 May [sic] they arrived for the first time, and the person who came was introduced herself to us as Ms or Miss Beatrice. We came out to be registered. When this was happening, I had an impression we were not supposed to be registered on that occasion, so we came into the area where we were taking meals. There was a table in the hallway in the building B, and Ms Beatrice asked me when I was captured. I told her the date of my capture. She was surprised and she asked me, "So how come you have not been registered yet?" I said that I did not know -- I gained the impression that she had been there before in the camp, but that they did not want to show me to her, which was the practice in the camp -- certain prisoners were not shown. So we were registered that time, and she asked all the prisoners whether there was anyone there who was in need of medical care. Among others I reported for medical care, because you could see bruises on my face. She asked me where I got that, and I told her that I accidentally hit myself with a shovel. I knew if I told her I had been beaten that I would be punished, so I told her I injured myself with a shovel while digging and that I needed medical care, because I have pains in my back. However, I subsequently received no medical care and the next day I was taken to dig again and we dug that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this Red Cross lady came and spoke to you, was the camp commander, Mr. Aleksovski, there at any stage during the time that she spoke to you, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to the hallway, we were registered and we were interviewed by the representatives of the ICRC and Mr. Aleksovski was present. He had some conversation with the gentleman from the ICRC. We did not listen in and, after that, these gentlemen from the ICRC requested Mr. Aleksovski to leave the room and she wanted to talk to us alone and then she asked us what the conditions were in the camp, what the food was like, whether we were taken to perform any kind of labour, what was it that we did, so she asked a number of things on what was going on in the camp, whether there were any killings taking place, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you prepared to tell her at that stage -- answer all of her questions that she asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only myself, but not one of the prisoners dared to talk about it, because we knew that they did not come to take us for an exchange, but only to come and talk to us, so that we could send a message to our families that we were alive. Nobody dared talk about these conditions in the camp, because we were suspicious of an interpreter who was with the ICRC, and later these suspicions proved true, after our first complaints and after we needed to go to see the doctor -- the lady from the ICRC, she did not speak any Bosnian and I do not know whether the interpreter did not want to interpret, or whether he did interpret and the gentleman from the camp refused to take us to be provided with medical care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just need to -- I think you said that it is recorded here on the transcript that you said this meeting was 24 and 25 May -- was it 24 and 25 May or was it earlier than that that she came first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When she first came, it was 24 or 25 April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned there that you had told her that you had gone trench digging, or you had been working, I am sorry, I think -- at least you mentioned that you had been trench digging. When did this first occur -- when did you first go to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went for the first time on my second day of staying at the Kaonik camp, in the morning. Mr. Stipo Andrijasevic in the camp came and told us to get up. He walked into the cell and told us to get up. We could not get up. We just looked at him from where we were lying and he yelled at us, "Why aren't you getting up" and we helped each other get up and we came out into the hallway. Then we were brought out in front of the building with the cells and Mr. Aleksovski and Mr. Krilic were there, and some other men in uniforms -- members of the HVO -- and then they put us in a van and drove us to the front-lines in the village of Strane to dig trenches for their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people that were selected to go and dig trenches at the front-line, did they appear to you to be selected randomly, or were they selected according to some system, or in some formal way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not at random. In my view, it could not have been random, because a list existed and if my name was on the list, I was selected to go and dig, so it was not by accident or random.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Strane on the front-line to dig these trenches, what happened then? When you got there, what did you see and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the front-line with the HVO, the group where I was supposed to dig in a truck on which an anti-aircraft gun was mounted and we were supposed to make it operational and we were given some tools to dig with. I was unable to work and the people who were in the group with me saw that I was in horrible shape and they told me, "You just move around a little bit here and pretend that you are digging, but do not really work". This is what went on until lunch arrived. With this meal, a group of soldiers arrived, led by a certain Zarko. I knew him from before in civilian life, from the town of Busovaca -- I know that he lived in the Kacun area. He arrived with this group of soldiers. Before we took our meal, he lined us up on a hill where we had been digging and he ordered us all to crouch. We did, and then Mr. Zarko went from one prisoner to the next and asked where we were from, how we were captured and things like that. He arrived -- he came to me and he asked me where I was from and I lied about the village that I was from. I did that, because I knew how I fared in the camp when I mentioned the name of my village, so I kind of assumed that I would fare the same if I repeated it. So I told him that I was from Vitez. Zarko had some kind of a rope in his hand and then he started whipping me with this rope and, as I sat down from these blows, he ordered me to crouch up again and he ordered one of his soldiers to bring a stick out of the forest. He brought a stick and he handed it to Zarko. He tested it by hitting the ground with it to test to see whether it was strong enough and it broke. Then he told the soldier to bring him a better one, so the soldier went back into the forest and brought another stick to Zarko. At that moment, I was expecting him to beat me with this stick and I expected a hard blow, but he surprised me and started hitting me with his fists and kicking me, so instead of a stick, he beat me this other way. Then he sent me down hill to go and have a meal. I went, but I could not even open my mouth properly -- I could not eat, so I just took a couple of bites -- I dipped in my pieces of bread in the mouth, and no sooner did I start eating, I was already summoned back to the soldiers, they surrounded me and the beatings started again on the part of the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why could you not eat, what was wrong with your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason why I could not eat was my mouth was swollen from this whipping of Zarko's with this rope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they brought you back, what did they do to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where back?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went down and had something to eat and then you said that, before you could even finish your meal, they brought you back. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then they told me to sit down. They pointed to a place where I was to sit down. Then they surrounded me and they started questioning me and started abusing me. Among the soldiers, I recognised one, because we went to school together and he told them that I was from this village, from where I come, and then, again, they started beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they beat you with on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me with whatever they had at hand. They also kicked me. I lost consciousness several times there, and as I would come to they would beat me again and so it went and then Zarko told me to go back up there and finish the job that we had started and that, after that, snipers were going to shoot at me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand by that when he said that snipers were going to shoot at you, what did you think he meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he had a sniper rifle in his hands and I understood that to mean that his sniper was not good enough, that he will test it on me, whether it is an accurate weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then after that, did you go back to start trench digging again, or start digging again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went up there, I was not able to dig, and then this group of people who were working with me came back and, a little while later, we were all told to assemble at a particular spot and we were told that every prisoner, that is, that two prisoners should each carry a box of spent cartridges or casings of shells to a particular place. When my turn came, I was told to carry a crate on my own, and it was filled with casings and they said, "If one of these casings falls out, we will kill you". We were supposed to go downhill and, thank God, I did not lose any of these casings, otherwise I do not know what would have happened. After that, we were again placed in a vehicle in which we came from the camp, and we were taken back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice it is now 1.30. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is time to break. We can stop here and resume tomorrow. Until tomorrow. (At 1.33pm the matter adjourned until Wednesday, 25th March 1998, at 9.00am) 22 23 24 25
